facts.text: A trade-off occurs when improving one goal worsens another; the Pareto front is the set of settings where no goal can be improved further without worsening another goal.
facts.quote: A trade-off is a situation where improving one goal worsens another, and the Pareto front is the set of settings where no goal can be improved any further without making some other goal worse.

facts.text: The Pareto front is named after economist Vilfredo Pareto.
facts.quote: the Pareto front, named after the economist Vilfredo Pareto

facts.text: The illustrative braking-settings example assumes that settings A, B and C all have zero misses in the critical scenarios.
facts.quote: Imagine three candidate settings, all with zero misses in the critical scenarios.

facts.text: In the illustrative braking-settings example, setting A brakes unnecessarily 2 times per 100 hours and stops with a generous margin.
facts.quote: Setting A brakes unnecessarily 2 times per 100 hours and stops with a generous margin.

facts.text: In the illustrative braking-settings example, setting B brakes unnecessarily 0.5 times per 100 hours but stops with a thinner margin.
facts.quote: Setting B brakes unnecessarily 0.5 times per 100 hours but stops with a thinner margin.

facts.text: In the illustrative braking-settings example, setting C brakes unnecessarily 1 time per 100 hours and has a stopping margin thinner than setting A's.
facts.quote: Setting C brakes unnecessarily 1 time per 100 hours with a margin thinner than A's.

facts.text: The illustrative braking-settings example describes setting C as dominated and discarded because C is worse than A on stopping margin and worse than B on nuisance braking.
facts.quote: C is worse than A on margin and worse than B on nuisance, so it is dominated and discarded.

facts.text: The illustrative braking-settings example places settings A and B on the Pareto front and treats choosing between them as a safety-policy decision.
facts.quote: A and B are both on the front; choosing between them is a safety-policy decision.

facts.text: The booklet recommends preserving and displaying the Pareto front rather than collapsing the trade-offs into one weighted score.
facts.quote: The booklet asks that the front be preserved and shown rather than collapsed into one weighted score.

facts.text: Evolutionary methods such as NSGA-II produce the whole Pareto front in one run but leave a policy decision about which Pareto point is acceptable.
facts.quote: Evolutionary methods such as NSGA-II produce the whole front in one run but "leave a policy decision over which Pareto point is acceptable".

facts.text: The booklet treats the policy choice among Pareto points as a benefit because the trade-off becomes a documented decision by the safety authority rather than a hidden weight chosen by an engineer.
facts.quote: The booklet treats that as a feature: the trade-off becomes a documented decision by the safety authority rather than a hidden weight chosen by an engineer [Chapter 9].

facts.text: Chapter 9 concludes that either a "no false brakes" target or a detection-only target produces a bad system, and that an explicit Pareto view is needed to keep both safety and productivity in sight.
facts.quote: Chapter 9 observes that a "no false brakes" target or a detection-only target each produce a bad system; only an explicit Pareto view keeps safety and productivity both in sight.

facts.text: Chapter 4 reports evidence that operators switch off systems with too many unnecessary stops; this gives the nuisance-braking axis safety weight in Chapter 9's trade-off analysis.
facts.quote: Chapter 4's evidence that operators switch off systems with too many unnecessary stops is why the nuisance axis carries safety weight [Chapter 4, Chapter 9].
